title: Learning a rule from a table
objectives: Choose the threshold that fits a table of examples best, and score it by how many it gets right.

screens.title: Drag the threshold
screens.prose: Here are the ten training emails. Spam sits on the top row, not spam on the bottom. The rule says spam to the right of the line. Drag $t$ and watch how many it gets right.

vlines.label: rule says spam to the right

screens.question: What is the most emails any threshold gets right?

hints.text: Drag $t$ from 0 to 10 and read the caption each time.
Try $t$ = 5.
At $t$ = 5 the rule gets 9 of 10 right; no threshold does better.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Try every whole-number $t$ and keep the best caption.

byKey.ten: No threshold gets all ten: the spam email with 2 links sits among not-spam emails.
byKey.eight: 8 comes at several thresholds, but $t$ = 5 does one better.

explain.text: The best threshold is 5, with 9 of 10 right. The one it misses is the spam email with only 2 links.

screens.title: Learning is choosing
screens.prose: Here is every threshold's score. The threshold is the model's one number. **Learning** is choosing it to get the most examples right. **Accuracy** is the number right over the total.
screens.question: What is the accuracy of the best threshold, as a percentage?

hints.text: Which bar is tallest?
$t$ = 5 gets 9 of 10.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the number right by the number of emails.

byKey.count: You typed 9 as a share of 100. Accuracy is 9 out of 10, which is 90%.
byKey.one-wrong: 10% is the share it gets wrong. Accuracy counts the right ones: 90%.

explain.text: The tallest bar is $t$ = 5 with 9 right. Accuracy is $\tfrac{9}{10} = 90\%$. Learning picked 5 because no other bar is as tall.

screens.title: Count it by hand: t = 3
screens.prose: Before the chart, someone has to count. Use the table and the rule **spam when links are at least 3**.
screens.question: How many of the ten does $t$ = 3 get right?

hints.text: Split the emails into those with fewer than 3 links and those with 3 or more.
Below 3: emails 1 to 4. The rule says not spam for them.
Below 3, three of four are not spam; at 3 or more, four of six are spam: $3 + 4 = 7$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count right answers on each side of the threshold, then add.

byKey.wrong-count: 3 is how many it gets wrong. The question asks for the right ones: $10 - 3 = 7$.
byKey.spam-side: You counted only the side where the rule says spam. Add the 3 right on the other side.
byKey.strict: You read the rule as more than 3. Email 5 has exactly 3 links, so the rule says spam and is wrong.

explain.text: Below 3 the rule says not spam: right for emails 1, 2 and 3, wrong for email 4. From 3 up it says spam: right for emails 7 to 10, wrong for 5 and 6. That is $3 + 4 = 7$.

screens.title: Count it by hand: t = 6
screens.prose: Now the rule **spam when links are at least 6**.
screens.question: How many of the ten does $t$ = 6 get right?

hints.text: Which emails have 6 links or more?
Emails 8, 9 and 10. All three are spam.
Below 6, five of seven are not spam: $5 + 3 = 8$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count each side, then add.

byKey.wrong-count: 2 is the number wrong, emails 4 and 7. Right is $10 - 2 = 8$.
byKey.spam-side: That is only the spam side. Add the 5 right on the not-spam side.

explain.text: At 6 or more: emails 8, 9 and 10, all spam, so 3 right. Below 6: right except emails 4 and 7, so 5. The total is 8, one fewer than $t$ = 5.

screens.title: A second feature
screens.prose: Try two features. The rule is now: **spam when links are at least 5, or when it says “free”**.
screens.question: How many of the ten does this rule get right?

hints.text: Which emails say “free”?
Emails 3, 4, 8 and 10 say “free”.
Email 4 is now caught, but email 3 says “free” and is not spam: 9 right.

feedback.correct: Still 9: it fixes email 4 and breaks email 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply the rule row by row.

byKey.ten: Email 3 says “free” and is not spam, so the new rule gets it wrong.
byKey.eight: Check email 4: it says “free”, so the new rule now calls it spam, which is right.

explain.text: The word “free” catches email 4, the spam that $t$ = 5 missed. But email 3 also says “free” and is not spam. The rule still gets 9 right: a second feature can help, but it does not have to.

screens.title: Half and half
screens.prose: A colleague says: “Pick the threshold that splits the emails in half. That is fair.” With $t$ = 4, five emails fall on each side.
screens.question: Which threshold should the model use?

options.text: $t$ = 4, which splits the emails in half
options.why: Splitting in half ignores the labels. $t$ = 4 gets 8 right; $t$ = 5 gets 9.
The average ignores the labels too. Learning picks the score, not the middle.
At 10 every email is called not spam: 5 of 10 right.

hints.text: What does learning choose the threshold for?
Compare the bars at 4 and 5.
5 scores 9, 4 scores 8.

feedback.correct: Learning keeps the threshold with the best score: 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the scores, not the middle of the data.

byKey.four: You split the link counts in half. That never looks at the labels, and it scores 8, not 9.

explain.text: The middle of the link counts says nothing about which emails are spam. Learning scores every threshold against the labels. $t$ = 5 wins with 9.

screens.title: Two winners
screens.prose: A smaller inbox of six emails. Here two thresholds tie.
screens.question: Thresholds 2 and 4 both get 5 of 6 right. Which should we choose?

options.text: Either: on this data they are equally good

options.why: $t$ = 3 scores only 4 of 6. A point between two winners need not be a winner.
Nothing in the data favours smaller. A fixed rule for ties is fine, but it is a choice.
Ties are normal with few examples. The data cannot tell these two apart.

hints.text: Do six emails give any reason to prefer one?
Both score 5; the data cannot separate them.

feedback.correct: Either will do on this data.

byKey.middle: You took the midpoint. Check it: at $t$ = 3 email 4 (3 links, not spam) is called spam and email 3 is missed. 4 of 6.

explain.text: Both thresholds make one mistake on these six emails. The data cannot tell them apart, so a script just needs a fixed rule, such as the smaller. More examples might break the tie.

screens.title: Count in code
screens.prose: Now teach Python to count. `links` and `labels` are lists of the same length, with 1 for spam and 0 for not.
screens.question: Write `count_correct(links, labels, t)`: the number of emails the rule “spam when links >= t” gets right.

widget.starter:
def count_correct(links, labels, t):
    # labels: 1 for spam, 0 for not spam
    right = 0
    # for each email, does the rule "spam when links >= t" agree with its label?
    return right
widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. Each result must equal the expected whole number.

hints.text: Loop over the positions with `for i in range(len(links)):`.
The rule says spam when `links[i] >= t`. The email is spam when `labels[i] == 1`.
Add 1 to `right` when the two agree: `if (links[i] >= t) == (labels[i] == 1):`.

feedback.correct: Your function counts agreements between the rule and the labels.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: At $t$ = 5 the answer is 9. If you got 4 or 5, you may be counting only spam or only not-spam emails.
byKey.test-4: At $t$ = 3 the answer is 7. If you got 8, check you used `>=`, not `>`.

explain.text:
For each email the rule gives a yes or no, and so does the label. Count the emails where they agree.

```python
if (links[i] >= t) == (labels[i] == 1):
    right = right + 1
```

screens.title: Choose in code
screens.prose: With `count_correct` written, choosing is a loop over thresholds that keeps the best so far. On a tie, keep the smaller threshold.
screens.question: Write `best_threshold(links, labels, ts)`: the `t` in the list `ts` with the most right, the smallest on a tie.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. Each result must equal the expected whole number.

hints.text: Keep two names: the best `t` so far and its count.
Loop over `sorted(ts)` so the smaller of two ties comes first.
Replace the best only when the new count is strictly bigger: `if right > best_right:`.

feedback.correct: Your loop keeps the best threshold and breaks ties towards the smaller.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: The thresholds come in reverse order here. Sort them, or compare `t` on a tie, so the smaller wins.
byKey.test-2: 2 and 4 tie on this inbox. If you got 4, you replaced the best on an equal count: use `>`, not `>=`.

explain.text:
Try each threshold, count, and keep the best. Using `>` means an equal count never replaces the earlier, smaller threshold.

```python
for t in sorted(ts):
    right = count_correct(links, labels, t)
    if right > best_right:
        best, best_right = t, right
```

screens.title: A desk's signal
screens.prose: A desk buys a share when its signal is above $t$, hoping it rises next day. Eight past days are shown. Three cut-offs are on the table: 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5.
screens.question: Which cut-off gets the most days right?

options.why: Count again at 1.0. Days 4, 6 and 8 are above it and all rose; four of the five below did not.
At 1.5 only day 8 is a buy. Days 3, 4 and 6 rose but were not bought.

hints.text: For each cut-off, count buys that rose and non-buys that did not.
At 1.0 the buys are days 4, 6 and 8.
1.0: 3 right buys and 4 right non-buys, 7 of 8.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Score each cut-off on all eight days.

explain.text: At 1.0 the rule buys on days 4, 6 and 8, which all rose. It skips five days, and four of those did not rise. That is 7 of 8, and how it does on new days is the next lesson's question.

ideas: The threshold is the model's one number; learning is choosing it to get the most examples right.
Accuracy is the number right over the total: 9 of 10 is 90%.
When two thresholds tie, the data cannot tell them apart; a script needs a fixed rule, such as the smaller.
